Devastating floods have destroyed the bridge over the Maumee River in the NORTH. Use your men to rebuild the BRIDGE. Supply the starving people of TOLEDO with 3 cars of desperately needed FOOD.

The economic boom is in full swing! Establish a link to LEXINGTON as quickly as possible and BUILD a MACHINE FACTORY there. The city of FRANKFORT is waiting for urgently needed MACHINES. But keep an eye on your competitor, William Blake. He wants to get a foot in this lucrative business, too!
Set up a monopoly in Kansas City.
Outdo your competitor William Blake and the Northern Railway and take CONTROL of KANSAS CITY. Gain a technological advantage and RESEARCH a new locomotive called the TENWHEELER in HANNIBAL.

Don't be bothered by the unrest of the Civil War. Stay alert and take advantage of the current political situation. Concentrate your activities on supporting FORT LAWRENCE in the WEST by supplying it with 5 cars of WEAPONS.

As you move to the west, reach the city of JACKSON - an important point in this stage of the game. Do whatever it takes to incorporate it into your railroad network and to keep the city under your control. Be sure to keep an eye out for a friendly old Indian. He could prove to be very helpful!
Establish a link to Provo City.

Watch out for acts of sabotage by the ruthless Northern Railway. A rail connection must be established to the cities of PRICE and PROVO CITY, which have been friendly toward you, as quickly as possible. And 6 cars of PETROLEUM would CEDAR CITY to join your side.
Forge ahead until you reach Elko.

The hunt for gold and oil is causing William Blake to fight with no holds barred. Defeat your opponent and establish a link to ELKO in the north and keep it under your control. Don't be fooled by the barren desert. Canyons that appear impossible to surmount and that the Northern Railway has already failed to cross lie ahead.

Finally! SAN FRANCISCO is within reach. Complete your masterpiece and finish building the first transcontinental railroad. Put William Blake and his company in their places and convey the first passengers there! But don't underestimate the mighty mountains that lie between us and the Pacific.

NEW YORK CITY, JANUARY 1, 1830

MISSION OBJECTIVE:
Learn the first steps that are necessary to become a successful railroad pioneer.

~ There still are no competitors
  that could get in your way.

PHILADELPHIA, MARCH 10, 1834

MISSION OBJECTIVE:
Establish a link to Pittsburgh and supply the city with an adequate quantity of timber.

~ Pennsylvania is known for its 
  green valleys and high mountains.

CLEVELAND, MAY 15, 1835

MISSION OBJECTIVE:
Build bridge and supply Toledo with food.


~ Ohio is known for its crystal-clear
  lakes.

HOPKINSVILLE, MAY 18, 1841

MISSION OBJECTIVE:
Build a machine factory in Lexington and deliver machines to Frankfort.

~ Beware! There is another railroad
  company.

SPRINGFIELD, JUNE 20, 1845

MISSION OBJECTIVE:
Win trade war in Kansas City and research locomotive in Hannibal.


~ All you'll find here are tranquil 
  expanses of prairie and flatlands.

ABILENE, FEBRUARY 1, 1851

MISSION OBJECTIVE:
A fort to the west must be supplied with weapons.

~ Cross the arid and merciless desert.

CHEYENNE,  APRIL 6, 1855

MISSION OBJECTIVE:
Establish a link to the city of Jackson despite the Indian blockade.

~ A competitor accompanies you
  on your difficult journey.

MONTEZUMA CREEK, APRIL 12, 1861

MISSION OBJECTIVE:
Establish a link between Price and Provo City and deliver petroleum to Cedar City. 

~ Be careful of your sneaky
  competitor.

LAS VEGAS, JULY 7, 1865

MISSION OBJECTIVE:
Build a bridge to Elko and add the city to the railroad network.

~ Stand up to the thankless 
  countryside and the dry desert.

SUSANVILLE, JULY 5, 1870

MISSION OBJECTIVE:
Establish a link to San Francisco and complete the railroad network.

~ A very powerful opponent and a
  mountain range await you at the end.

Lay track across Montana and take over as the most powerful railroad baron of all time.

(Mahatma Gandhi (1869 - 1948), Indian lawyer, statesman and reformer)

"If a seed could speak, it would complain that the 
painful part is germinating."

(Eduard Douwes Dekker (1820 - 1887) 
Dutch colonial official and writer)

Rough terrain calls for a great deal of skill when planning and laying your track.



"Mountains and valleys have a 
common enemy. The plains."

(Werner Mitsch (*1936), German Aphorist)

A frightful competition awaits you. 
Show your opponent who the real
trade king is in New Mexico.

"There are three reasons to fight in human nature.

self-confidence and the third is the thirst for glory."

(Thomas Hobbes (1588 - 1679), English philosopher)

Establish a link between all the cities in the state full of lakes.



"We often build bridges that we 
can jump from." 

(Oliver Tietze (*1965), German Aphorist)

Kick your opponent out and continue your journey through the narrow terrain with purpose.
Act carefully and be the first to deliver.
Show some pioneering spirit! Be the first to reach your destination!

text:
Well done. From where I sit, you're a born railroad pioneer. But from now on we're on our own. 

It's 1834 and we are in the beautiful state of Pennsylvania in the eastern part of the United States. This is the heartland of America, and scenic green countryside and glorious mountains await us. But so do a lot of problems. 

Since the War of Independence there has been an absolute shortage of raw materials here in Pennsylvania. Building materials, food and clothing are in short supply. And because of all the trouble brewing in Europe, large numbers of immigrants are moving to the United States. 

It is up to us to help the people rebuild and secure their livelihood. We must make sure that goods are distributed regularly and arrive where they are needed most.

According to my information, we still don't have to worry about competition, although it's only a matter of time before we get some company!

The people in Pittsburgh can breathe a sigh of relief. The timber they received should give them enough building materials to build shelter. You have my appreciation!
According to the calendar, it is the year 1835 and we are in the rainy state of Ohio, the Indian name for "something big" - hopefully it's not too big for us to handle! 

The new settlements are in full swing and demanding everything the economy has to offer. Cities are springing up out of the ground like mushrooms, and the local suppliers of raw materials are on the verge of collapse. Food manufacturers in particular are hoping for our support by building the railroad. 
A state of emergency already exists in some cities. They desperately need our assistance.

We also received a message about another railroad company that is working its way toward us. Look's like we're going to get some competition.

The industry in Kentucky is stronger than ever, which is entirely because of you and the railroad. We have also managed to take a small lead over the competition. Keep it up!
It is now the year 1845 and we have pushed forward to Missouri. Thanks to our good planning, we are now crossing the rolling prairie and will be able to avoid the mighty glaciers. 
Industrialization continues and Missouri appears to be a simple, easy-to-develop piece of land. However, the dark signs of a nearing war have taken on alarming proportions. Weapons are in great demand, and the local Indians are a feared enemy. 

I have a newspaper article here reporting that our competitor has made his first delivery. This is getting serious!

Missouri is behind us, and Kansas City is under our control. You have my respect. Once again you have done a good job and dealt our competitor a decisive blow. 

The year is 1851. The next round - Kansas and Nebraska - won't be easy. Prepare yourself for the barren desert that knows no mercy. I really hope we get through this one alive.

The Civil War is raging on, and the innocent Indians aren't the only ones who are suffering because of it. 
The railroad could play a key role in deciding the outcome of the war and benefit from the situation at the same time. Weapons and raw materials that are difficult to transport using other means of transportation are needed throughout the country.

It turns out that the competing railroad company sympathizes with the southern states and is sending them reinforcements. We have to do something to stop them.

We did it. I take my hat off to you! Boy, the way you managed to get us through that was unbelievable!
It is now the year 1855 and we are in Wyoming, which in the language of the Delaware Indians means "Land of the Great Plain". But don't let that fool you. There are plenty of really big mountains here, too.

As we continue to move westward, our scouts are reporting more frequent clashes with the Indians. They are worried about their very survival and refuse to leave their land under any circumstances. Although they have no reason to be afraid of us, the city of Jackson, for example, has been cut off by the Indians. It looks like a real problem -- but not one that can't be solved somehow.

I heard that our competitor is experiencing the same problems we are, but he is using weapons to deal with the Indians. He's even more unscrupulous than I thought.

That was quite an accomplishment. The people of the city of Jackson can sleep peacefully again and the Indians have lay down their weapons.

It is now 1861 and we are in a city with a history: The area now known as Utah was inhabited by Indian tribes as far back as 9000 BC. But there is no need for us to be afraid of them now.

The economy is stabile and raw materials are available in abundance. But other people are taking advantage of the situation, too. Gangs of bandits are lurking everywhere, and the area is under their control. It's obvious that our competitor is in cahoots with the scoundrels.

We had better prepare for the worst. I heard that several wagon trains have been sabotaged or robbed in eastern Utah.

I like it when you do that.  The cities of Price and Provo City will be in your debt forever. And given all your strengths, the competition doesn't stand a chance.

The year is 1865 and we are in Nevada, which is also known as the Silver State. That sounds pretty promising to me!

The race between us and the competition is getting more and more newspaper coverage. There is all this wild speculation about who will be victorious and who will come up short. The rumors about gold deposits have given rise to mass hysteria and made an already difficult situation worse. 

The competition has caught back up to us again. Tensions are high on all fronts, and we're being challenged to an open battle. It's more important than ever that we put our opponent in his place.

That was damned close! We managed to reach Elko before the competition and help the people there in time. But the rescue operation cost us some valuable time.

It is 1875 and we have almost reached our goal. The last part of our journey lies before us: California, the Golden State with the mighty Sierra Nevada. This is the home of the highest mountain in the United States -- Mount Whitney, which is a proud 4,417 meters high. Now our tunnel builders and geologists have to show us what they're made of.

The finish line is within reach. But the opposition is already a dangerous step ahead of us. For days those scoundrels have been on the other side of a huge mountain that still lies before us.

San Francisco has been working feverishly to prepare for the railroad's arrival with a festive ceremony. I pray to God that your capabilities make us the hero in this story.

This is the story of some of the most courageous men and one of the most daring enterprises ever attempted by mankind. 

It is the story of great railroad companies that had but one goal: to build the first transcontinental railroad straight across the unexplored America of the 19th century. They were brave pioneers who entered into a race against time and exposed themselves to unbelievable dangers. Even if it meant losing their lives.

The unfathomable expanse of a wild, rough continent lay before an army of inexperienced workers. They had to overcome massive mountains with snow-covered passes, gaping canyons and merciless deserts. 
And competing railroad companies harassed each other, too. Acts of sabotage and underhanded attacks would soon become part of the sorrow-filled lives of the railroad pioneers.

The battle for wealth, fame and honor had begun.

text: This year's bazaar will be even better than it was last year. The organizers thank you for delivering the textiles on time. You receive $14,000.
Switch messages in this category on / off

1. Interface

GAME COMMANDS

Mouse wheel / Page UP, Page DOWN
~ Zoom (screen section & mini-map)

PAUSE: 			
~ Pause / continue game

ESC:
~ To main menu

Left mouse button:
~ Select buildings and objects

Right mouse button:
~ Press and hold to move screen section

2. Laying track

ESTABLISH RAIL LINK TO NEIGHBORING CITY

~Select unfinished end of track
~Click destinations directly or use arrows to help plan route
~Lay track to neighboring city
~Double-click on train station or on station symbol in track-laying interface
~Confirm your selection with the green OK button
~Wait until the train station is finished

3. Assemble troop

ASSEMBLE A TROOP

~Select the white building, i.e. the geographers' district.
~Assemble a troop (drag + drop / double-click)
~Select a pioneer, a prospector and a trapper for the troop
~Confirm your selection with the green OK button
~Close the menu with the red CANCEL button

4. Eliminate danger

ELIMINATE LOOMING DANGER

~ Select your exploration troop
~ Move your troop to the middle of the danger zone (double-click / arrows + OK) 
~ Use your trapper to eliminate the danger

5. Evaluate resource field

EVALUATE THE RESOURCE FIELD

~Select an exploration troop
~Move your troop to the corn field (double-click / arrow + OK) 
~Use your prospector to evaluate the corn field

6. Link resource field to resource field

BUILD A TRAIN STATION AT THE CORN FIELD

~Select unfinished end of the track
~Lay track up to the cornfield
~Build station (double-click / station symbol in track-laying interface)
~Confirm your selection with the green OK button

7. Build six-wheeler locomotive

BUILD THE SIX-WHEELER LOCOMOTIVE

~Select the industrial district (green building) in NEW YORK CITY
~Click on the first locomotive in the table
~Confirm the building order with the green OK button
~Wait for the locomotive to be completed

8. Build passenger car and freight car

BUILD A PASSENGER AND A FREIGHT CAR

~Select the industrial district (green building) in New York City
~Switch to the menu for building cars (upper left button)
~Select the passenger car in the table
~Confirm your building order with the green OK button
~Wait for the passenger car to be completed
~Then build a freight car (1)

9. Dispatch train

DRIVE TRAIN TO CORN FIELD

~Select the train station (blue building) in NEW YORK CITY
~Select the six-wheeler locomotive for your train (double-click)
~Attach the passenger and freight cars to the train (double-click)
~Select the waiting passengers (double-click)
~Select the CORN FIELD (1) as the train's destination
~Dispatch the train on the planned route with the green OK button
~Wait until the train arrives at the corn field

10. Transport corn to New York City

ESTABLISH A PERMANENT TRADE ROUTE

~Select the station at the corn field
~Load corn in the freight car (double-click)
~Select NEW YORK CITY as the train's destination 
~Now select NEW YORK CITY in the route planner above your train
~As an option, you may also select waiting passengers (double-click)
~Select the corn field as the destination to close the trade circuit 
~Activate the trade route using the button (upper right) that has just become available
~Dispatch the train on the scheduled trade route with the green OK button
